result.title: Merge Booking Ranges
result.description:
A meeting room keeps a list of bookings. Each booking is a pair `[start, end]` with
`start <= end`, both integers. Bookings that overlap or **touch** (one ends exactly when the
next starts) should be shown as a single block.

Write `merge_ranges(bookings)` that returns the merged blocks, sorted by start time.

:::figure{caption="Bookings [1,3], [2,6] and [8,10] become [1,6] and [8,10]"}
<svg viewBox="0 0 330 70" width="330" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" font-family="monospace" font-size="11">
  <line x1="10" y1="60" x2="320" y2="60" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1"/>
  <rect x="40" y="8" width="60" height="12" fill="none" stroke="currentColor"/>
  <rect x="70" y="24" width="120" height="12" fill="none" stroke="currentColor"/>
  <rect x="250" y="8" width="60" height="12" fill="none" stroke="currentColor"/>
  <rect x="40" y="42" width="150" height="8" fill="currentColor" opacity="0.35"/>
  <rect x="250" y="42" width="60" height="8" fill="currentColor" opacity="0.35"/>
</svg>
:::

### Example

```text
Input:  bookings = [[1, 3], [2, 6], [8, 10], [10, 12]]
Output: [[1, 6], [8, 12]]
```

### Constraints

- $0 \le n \le 10^5$
- $-10^9 \le start \le end \le 10^9$
- The input is **not** necessarily sorted. Don't modify the input list.

:::note
Aim for $O(n \log n)$ time.
:::
hints: What becomes easy if the bookings are sorted by start time?
After sorting, compare each booking with the last merged block only.
Touching counts as overlapping, so use `<=` when comparing the next start with the current end.

result.title: Iterators, Await, and the Two Kinds of Suspension
Iterators, Await, and the Two Kinds of Suspension
result.description:
Python has **two** different things that can pause, and confusing them is the most common
async bug. This problem climbs the whole ladder — plain iterators, then `await`, then async
generators — so you can tell the two apart by building each one.

| | what pauses | control goes to | resumes when |
|---|---|---|---|
| **generator frame** | a `yield` | the consumer (`next()` / `async for`) | the consumer asks for the next item |
| **task** | an `await` of something *still pending* | the event loop | that awaitable completes |

Three consequences, each tested below:

1. One `next()` runs the body up to exactly **one** `yield`. The frame really is frozen.
2. Freezing a frame is **not** the same as giving the event loop a turn. `async for` over a
   generator that never awaits is a tight loop with no scheduling points at all.
3. Anything written **after** a `yield` may never run, because the consumer can walk away.
   Cleanup belongs in `finally`.

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant L as event loop
    participant C as consumer
    participant G as async generator
    C->>G: __anext__()
    G->>G: await asyncio.sleep(0)
    Note over L,G: the await suspends the TASK
    L-->>G: resumed
    G-->>C: yield n
    Note over C,G: the yield suspends the FRAME only
```

## 1. `Peekable` — the sync iterator protocol

```python
class Peekable:
    def __init__(self, items: Iterable[T]) -> None: ...
    def __iter__(self) -> Peekable: ...
    def __next__(self) -> T: ...
    def peek(self) -> T: ...
```

`peek()` returns the next item **without consuming it**, so the following `next()` returns that
same item.

- `iter(p) is p` — an iterator is its own iterable.
- `peek()` can be called repeatedly; it returns the same item every time.
- Once exhausted, both `peek()` and `next()` raise `StopIteration` — every time, not just the
  first.
- `items` may be a **one-shot** iterator (a generator, a file handle, a stream), so you cannot
  use `len()`, indexing or `list()` to look ahead. You have to buffer one item.

## 2. `take` — a sync generator, and who runs between resumes

```python
def take(items: Iterable[T], k: int) -> Iterator[T]
```

Yield at most `k` items from `items`, stopping early if the source runs out.

- Constructing the generator runs no code; nothing is read before the first `next()`.
- Each `next()` advances the source by **exactly one** item.
- `k <= 0` yields nothing and never touches `items`.

There is no `await` anywhere on this rung. Watch the interleaving, with a source that logs
every time it hands out an item:

```text
log = []
g = take(source, 3)
next(g)  ->  source logs "step",  caller logs "got 1"
next(g)  ->  source logs "step",  caller logs "got 2"
next(g)  ->  source logs "step",  caller logs "got 3"
```

The generator's frame froze at the `yield` and **the caller kept running** before asking for
the next item. That is "one `next()` = one `yield`", and it needs no event loop at all.

## 3. `fair_countdown` — an async generator that actually suspends

```python
async def fair_countdown(n: int) -> AsyncIterator[int]
```

Yield `n, n-1, ..., 1`, calling `await asyncio.sleep(0)` **before each** item.

The position of that line is the whole lesson, and only a scheduling test can see it. With one
other task taking two turns:

```text
fair_countdown(2):  ['other', 2, 'other', 1]
```

Every item is gated — no value is delivered until the loop has given somebody else a turn,
including the *first* one.

:::note
`await asyncio.sleep(0)` is not a timer. Internally it is a bare `yield` aimed at the **task
driver** instead of at a consumer. Same keyword, different recipient, completely different
consequence.
:::

## 4. `burst` — the control group

```python
async def burst(n: int) -> AsyncIterator[int]
```

Yield `n, n-1, ..., 1` with **no `await` anywhere**.

This is the anti-pattern, kept deliberately so the difference is measurable:

```text
burst(2):           [2, 1, 'other', 'other']
```

It is a perfectly valid async generator and still yields one item per `__anext__()`. But each
of those calls completes **synchronously**, so the consumer drains every item inside one task
step, and the other task does not get a turn until the generator is exhausted.

:::warning
An async generator that never awaits is indistinguishable, to the scheduler, from
`iter([n, n-1, ..., 1])`. It only becomes cooperative where it awaits something pending.
:::

## 5. `drain` — cleanup that always runs

```python
async def drain(conn: Connection) -> AsyncIterator[str]
```

`conn.readline()` is `async` and returns `None` at end of input; `conn.close()` is a plain
method. Yield each line with surrounding whitespace stripped, skipping empty lines.
`conn.close()` must be called **exactly once**, whether the consumer reads everything, breaks
out early, or `readline()` raises.

:::details{summary="Why does cleanup written after the loop fail?"}
When the consumer leaves early, the generator is paused **at the `yield`**. Python later calls
`aclose()`, which throws `GeneratorExit` there. Statements after your loop are never reached;
only a `finally` block runs.

```python
async def good(conn):
    try:
        while (line := await conn.readline()) is not None:
            yield line.strip()
    finally:
        conn.close()              # always runs

async def bad(conn):
    while (line := await conn.readline()) is not None:
        yield line.strip()
    conn.close()                  # skipped on an early break
```
:::

## Worked example

`fair_countdown(2)` and `burst(2)`, each racing one other task that takes two turns:

```text
fair_countdown      await sleep(0)   other: 'other'
                    yield 2          consumer: 2
                    await sleep(0)   other: 'other'
                    yield 1          consumer: 1
result  ['other', 2, 'other', 1]

burst               yield 2          consumer: 2
                    yield 1          consumer: 1
                    (exhausted)      other: 'other', 'other'
result  [2, 1, 'other', 'other']
```

## Constraints

- `0 <= n <= 10_000` for both countdowns, and `0 <= k <= 10_000` for `take`.
- Use `asyncio.sleep(0)` — never a real delay. The tests assert exact interleavings.
- Standard library only. `test_visible.py` shows some of the tests.
hints:
`Peekable` needs one slot of state: the buffered item and whether that slot is filled.
`__next__` returns the buffer when it is filled and pulls from the source otherwise.
`__iter__` returns `self`.
`take`: call `iter(items)` once, then loop over `range(max(k, 0))`, pull one item with
`next()` inside `try/except StopIteration: return`, and `yield` what you pulled.
In `fair_countdown` the only difference from `burst` is where the `await` sits — it must be
*before* the `yield`, not after it and not missing. In `drain`, wrap the whole `while` loop
in `try: ... finally: conn.close()`.

import asyncio
from typing import AsyncIterator, Iterable, Iterator, Protocol, TypeVar

T = TypeVar("T")


class Connection(Protocol):
    async def readline(self) -> str | None: ...
    def close(self) -> None: ...


class Peekable:
    """A sync iterator that can look one step ahead without consuming."""

    def __init__(self, items: Iterable[T]) -> None:
        raise NotImplementedError

    def __iter__(self) -> "Peekable":
        raise NotImplementedError

    def __next__(self) -> T:
        raise NotImplementedError

    def peek(self) -> T:
        raise NotImplementedError


def take(items: Iterable[T], k: int) -> Iterator[T]:
    """Yield at most k items from items, reading lazily."""
    raise NotImplementedError
    yield  # keep this a generator function


async def fair_countdown(n: int) -> AsyncIterator[int]:
    """Yield n, n-1, ..., 1, awaiting asyncio.sleep(0) before EACH item."""
    raise NotImplementedError
    yield


async def burst(n: int) -> AsyncIterator[int]:
    """Yield n, n-1, ..., 1 with no await at all. Used as the control group."""
    raise NotImplementedError
    yield


async def drain(conn: Connection) -> AsyncIterator[str]:
    """Yield stripped non-empty lines, closing conn exactly once."""
    raise NotImplementedError
    yield

"""Visible tests, one worked example per question type.

The five question types are declared as pytest classes, so the run results show
them as collapsible section headers instead of one flat list:

    1. TestValuesAndOrder    does it produce the right items, in order?
    2. TestIteratorProtocol  is it really an iterator - iter(), peek(), StopIteration?
    3. TestLaziness          is anything read before it is asked for?
    4. TestTaskSuspension    does an await hand the loop a turn?
    5. TestCleanup           does close() run on every exit path?

`TestTaskSuspension` gets a deliberately weak example: it only checks that the
other task ran before the first item. The exact interleaving is graded in
test_hidden.py.
"""

import asyncio

from solution import Peekable, burst, drain, fair_countdown, take


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Helpers - also imported by test_hidden.py
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------


class FakeConn:
    """An async line source that counts how many times it was closed."""

    def __init__(self, lines):
        self.lines = list(lines)
        self.closed = 0

    async def readline(self):
        await asyncio.sleep(0)
        return self.lines.pop(0) if self.lines else None

    def close(self):
        self.closed += 1


class LogSource:
    """A one-shot iterator that records every time it is stepped."""

    def __init__(self, items, log):
        self._it = iter(items)
        self.log = log

    def __iter__(self):
        return self

    def __next__(self):
        self.log.append("step")
        return next(self._it)


async def collect(agen):
    """Drain an async generator into a list."""
    return [x async for x in agen]


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 1. Values and order
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------


class TestValuesAndOrder:
    """Does it produce the right items, in the right order?"""

    async def test_fair_countdown_values(self):
        """fair_countdown(n) yields n, n-1, ..., 1"""
        assert await collect(fair_countdown(3)) == [3, 2, 1]

    async def test_burst_values(self):
        """burst(n) yields the same values; only *when* they arrive differs"""
        assert await collect(burst(3)) == [3, 2, 1]


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 2. Iterator protocol
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------


class TestIteratorProtocol:
    """Is it really an iterator - iter(), peek(), StopIteration?"""

    def test_peekable_peek_lookahead(self):
        """peek() shows the next item without consuming it"""
        p = Peekable([1, 2])
        assert iter(p) is p
        assert p.peek() == 1
        assert p.peek() == 1
        assert next(p) == 1
        assert next(p) == 2


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 3. Laziness
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------


class TestLaziness:
    """Is anything read before it is asked for?"""

    def test_take_is_lazy(self):
        """take() reads nothing until the first next()"""
        log = []

        def source():
            for i in [1, 2, 3]:
                log.append("read")
                yield i

        g = take(source(), 2)
        assert log == []
        assert next(g) == 1
        assert log == ["read"]


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 4. Task suspension
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------


class TestTaskSuspension:
    """Does an await hand the event loop a turn?"""

    async def test_await_lets_the_other_task_run_first(self):
        """the first value arrives only after another task has had a turn

        Deliberately weaker than the hidden tests: this only checks that the
        other task ran *before* the first item. The exact interleaving for both
        countdowns is what the hidden tests grade - see the description's
        "Worked example" for the full expected order.
        """
        seen = []

        async def other():
            seen.append("other")
            await asyncio.sleep(0)

        async def consume():
            async for n in fair_countdown(3):
                seen.append(n)

        await asyncio.gather(consume(), other())
        assert seen.index("other") < seen.index(3)


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 5. Cleanup
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------


class TestCleanup:
    """Does close() run on every exit path, exactly once?"""

    async def test_drain_strips_and_closes(self):
        """drain() strips, skips blanks, and closes the connection"""
        conn = FakeConn([" a \n", "\n", "b\n"])
        assert await collect(drain(conn)) == ["a", "b"]
        assert conn.closed == 1

result.title: Decode with a KV Cache
result.description:
An autoregressive transformer generates one token at a time. At step $t$ the new token's query attends to the keys and values of **every** position $0..t$. Recomputing $K$ and $V$ for the whole prefix at every step repeats work: step $t$ re-projects $t$ old tokens. A **KV cache** stores each position's key and value the first time they're computed. Each decode step then projects only the new token, appends its $k, v$ to the cache, and attends over the cached tensors. ```mermaid flowchart LR x["x_t (new token)"] --> P["project: q_t, k_t, v_t"] P -->|append k_t, v_t| C[("KV cache
[B, H, t+1, Dh]")] P -->|q_t| A["attend(q_t, K, V)"] C -->|K, V| A A --> o[o_t] ``` For one head with head size $d_h$: $$o_t = \operatorname{softmax}\!\left(\frac{q_t K_{0..t}^\top}{\sqrt{d_h}}\right) V_{0..t}$$ ### Your task In `solution.py`: 1. **`KVCache`** preallocates key and value buffers of shape `[batch, n_heads, max_len, head_dim]` on the given device. - `append(k, v)` writes `t_new` new positions (`k`, `v` are `[batch, n_heads, t_new, head_dim]`) and raises `ValueError` if the cache would go past `max_len`. - `get()` returns `(k, v)` for the positions written so far. Return slices of the buffers (views), not copies. - `len(cache)` is the number of positions written so far. 2. **`decode_with_cache(x, w_q, w_k, w_v, n_heads)`** processes `x` (`[B, T, D]`) **one position at a time**, using a `KVCache` and the read-only helpers in `attention.py`. It returns the attention output `[B, T, D]`, where row $t$ attends to positions $0..t$ (causal). Projections are `x @ w_q`, `x @ w_k`, `x @ w_v`, each with weight shape `[D, D]`. :::note `attend()` only accepts a single query position, so a full-sequence shortcut won't work. Tests run on the selected device (`mps` on Apple silicon, `cuda` on NVIDIA). Keep every tensor on `x.device`. ::: :::details{summary="Why preallocate?"} Growing the cache with `torch.cat` at every step allocates a new tensor and copies the whole prefix each time, which is $O(T^2)$ memory traffic. Writing into a preallocated buffer keeps each step $O(1)$ apart from the attention itself. Real inference engines go further and page the cache into fixed-size blocks. :::
hints: In `__init__`: `self.k = torch.zeros(batch, n_heads, max_len, head_dim, device=device, dtype=dtype)`, the same for `v`, and `self.length = 0`.
Decode loop: `x_t = x[:, t:t+1]` keeps the time dimension. Project it, `split_heads`, append, `attend`, `merge_heads`, then collect the outputs and `torch.cat` them along dim 1.

result.title: Your First CUDA Kernel
result.description:
A CUDA **kernel** is a function that runs on the GPU, many copies at once. Each copy is a
**thread** with its own index. Threads are grouped into **blocks**, and blocks form a **grid**.
You choose the shape when you launch the kernel:

```cpp
my_kernel<<<num_blocks, threads_per_block>>>(args...);
```

Inside the kernel, a thread computes its global index from built-in variables:

$$i = \texttt{blockIdx.x} \cdot \texttt{blockDim.x} + \texttt{threadIdx.x}$$

:::figure{caption="A grid of 3 blocks with 4 threads each covers indices 0-11"}
<svg viewBox="0 0 372 64" width="372" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" font-family="monospace" font-size="10">
  <g fill="none" stroke="currentColor">
    <rect x="2" y="16" width="120" height="30"/><rect x="126" y="16" width="120" height="30"/><rect x="250" y="16" width="120" height="30"/>
  </g>
  <g fill="currentColor" opacity="0.25">
    <rect x="6" y="20" width="26" height="22"/><rect x="35" y="20" width="26" height="22"/><rect x="64" y="20" width="26" height="22"/><rect x="93" y="20" width="26" height="22"/>
    <rect x="130" y="20" width="26" height="22"/><rect x="159" y="20" width="26" height="22"/><rect x="188" y="20" width="26" height="22"/><rect x="217" y="20" width="26" height="22"/>
    <rect x="254" y="20" width="26" height="22"/><rect x="283" y="20" width="26" height="22"/><rect x="312" y="20" width="26" height="22"/><rect x="341" y="20" width="26" height="22"/>
  </g>
  <g fill="currentColor"><text x="40" y="11">block 0</text><text x="164" y="11">block 1</text><text x="288" y="11">block 2</text>
  <text x="14" y="58">0</text><text x="43" y="58">1</text><text x="72" y="58">2</text><text x="101" y="58">3</text><text x="138" y="58">4</text><text x="355" y="58">11</text></g>
</svg>
:::

### Your task

In `kernel.cu`:

1. Write the kernel `vector_add(a, b, c, n)` that sets `c[i] = a[i] + b[i]` for every
   `i < n`. The grid is usually bigger than `n`, so threads with `i >= n` must do nothing.
2. Write `launch_vector_add(d_a, d_b, d_c, n)`. It receives **device** pointers and launches
   the kernel with 256 threads per block and enough blocks to cover all `n` elements:
   $\lceil n / 256 \rceil$, or `(n + 255) / 256` in integer arithmetic.

The hidden harness allocates the device memory, copies the inputs, calls your launcher, and
checks every element against a CPU computation. Sizes include `n = 1` and sizes that aren't a
multiple of 256.

:::warning
This problem needs an NVIDIA GPU. Run it on a CUDA executor: a local Linux machine, or a remote
SSH or SLURM machine configured in `~/.config/leegen/executors.yaml`.
:::
hints: Inside the kernel: `int i = blockIdx.x * blockDim.x + threadIdx.x; if (i < n) c[i] = a[i] + b[i];`
Launcher: `int blocks = (n + 255) / 256; vector_add<<<blocks, 256>>>(d_a, d_b, d_c, n);`

result.title: Tiled Matrix Multiply in WebGPU
result.description:
Multiply an $m \times k$ matrix $A$ by a $k \times n$ matrix $B$:

$$C_{rc} = \sum_{i=0}^{k-1} A_{ri}\, B_{ic}$$

All matrices are `f32`, stored **row-major** in flat arrays (`A[r][i]` is `a[r * k + i]`).
The host launches a 2-D grid of $16 \times 16$ workgroups, one invocation per element of $C$:
`gid.x` is the column and `gid.y` is the row.

### Why tile

A naive kernel reads $2k$ values from storage for each output. Neighbouring invocations read
the same rows and columns again and again. Tiling loads each $16 \times 16$ block of $A$ and of
$B$ into `var<workgroup>` memory **once per workgroup**, and every invocation reuses it 16
times:

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    subgraph per tile t
        LA["load A block (row tile, column tile t)"] --> BAR1[workgroupBarrier]
        LB["load B block (row tile t, column tile)"] --> BAR1
        BAR1 --> MAC["16 multiply-adds from workgroup memory"]
        MAC --> BAR2[workgroupBarrier]
    end
    BAR2 -->|next t| LA
    BAR2 -->|done| W["write C[row][col] when inside m x n"]
```

Pad with zeros when a block reaches past the edge of $A$ or $B$. Matrix sizes are not
multiples of 16, and every invocation must still reach both barriers, including those outside
$C$.

:::note
**If you know CUDA:** this is the classic shared-memory tiled SGEMM. Here `tile_a` and
`tile_b` are `__shared__ float[16][16]`, and the two barriers are the two `__syncthreads()`
calls.
:::

### Bindings

| Binding | Variable | Contents |
|---|---|---|
| 0 | `a: array<f32>` (read) | $A$, $m \cdot k$ values |
| 1 | `b: array<f32>` (read) | $B$, $k \cdot n$ values |
| 2 | `c: array<f32>` (read_write) | $C$, $m \cdot n$ values |
| 3 | `dims: Dims` (uniform) | `m`, `k`, `n` |

The host passes $A$ and $B$ as lists of rows and returns $C$ as a list of rows. The comparison
uses a relative tolerance. On the largest case it also reports the GPU time of your kernel
(timestamp queries, rounded by the browser to about 0.1 ms) as a metric.

### Example

```text
A = [[1, 2],      B = [[5, 6],      C = [[19, 22],
     [3, 4]]           [7, 8]]           [43, 50]]
```
hints: Start with a correct naive kernel (loop over `i`, read `a` and `b` directly), then add tiling.
Per tile `t`, invocation (lid.x, lid.y) loads `A[row][t*16 + lid.x]` into `tile_a[lid.y][lid.x]` and `B[t*16 + lid.y][col]` into `tile_b[lid.y][lid.x]`, or 0 when out of range.
The tile loop runs `(k + 15) / 16` times for every invocation. Don't return early for invocations outside C; only skip the final write.
